mcqs.question: What does tracing the wait-for cycle actually require, beyond naming the four deadlock conditions?
options: Counting the exact number of threads involved in the program
Measuring the total CPU time each thread has consumed
Following each thread's held lock to what it's waiting for, and that lock's holder, until the loop closes back on the starting thread
Listing every lock declared anywhere in the codebase, regardless of whether it's involved
mcqs.explanation: The four conditions only explain why deadlock is possible in general; identifying this specific bug means following the actual chain of holds-and-waits-for until it closes into a loop. Thread count and CPU time aren't part of the diagnosis, and unrelated locks elsewhere in the codebase don't matter.

mcqs.question: In the transferTo deadlock example, what determines the lock acquisition order for a given thread?
options: The order fields are declared in the Account class
Which account's transferTo method the thread called first — this.lock is always acquired before to.lock
Whichever account has the larger balance at the time of the call
mcqs.explanation: transferTo always locks this before to, so the order depends purely on which account's method was invoked — two threads calling in opposite directions lock in opposite orders. Field declaration order, thread priority, and balance size play no role in which lock is acquired first.

mcqs.question: What can a thread dump or JVM deadlock detector tell you that lock-contention metrics alone can't?
options: The average time every lock in the system has been held historically
Which lock will deadlock next, before it actually happens
The total number of times a lock has ever been acquired since JVM startup
The exact threads and locks currently stuck in a closed wait-for cycle, right now
mcqs.explanation: A thread dump directly reports which threads are stuck in a cycle and on which locks, at this exact moment — a definitive after-the-fact diagnosis. Contention metrics only show wait-time trends, not a confirmed cycle, and neither tool predicts a future deadlock before it happens.

mcqs.question: Why is wrapping the whole transferTo method in one global lock shared by every account a bad fix for the deadlock?
options: It requires rewriting Account to store all balances in a single class
It changes the balance calculation formula used during a transfer
It serializes every transfer in the system through one lock, even between completely unrelated accounts, destroying throughput to fix a narrow cycle
It makes the deadlock happen more often instead of preventing it
mcqs.explanation: A single global lock does remove the cycle, but at the cost of forcing every transfer anywhere in the system to queue behind one lock, even between accounts that never interact — a much larger cost than the narrow fix needed. It requires no rewrite of Account's storage, no formula change, and it does prevent the deadlock, just wastefully.
